Vignette:
# Fadi's Vigil

Fadi Mansour was fifty-eight when the shelling began in earnest. He had been working with the international relief organization for three years by then, moving between field hospitals in a country he had left as a boy but never quite stopped thinking of as home. The work gave him purpose—something his divorce had stripped away five years earlier, something his political career in Massachusetts had never quite provided despite two decades in the state legislature. In the hospital, there was clarity: bodies needed help, medicine was needed, and he could deliver both.

The day that changed everything started like most others. Fadi was in the supply tent checking inventory when the first blast came—not close, but close enough that the ground trembled beneath his feet. He remembers the smell first, before anything else: burnt rubber and something charred he did not want to identify. His colleague Hassan was beside him. They had been laughing about something trivial moments before. The second blast was different. It was closer. The tent collapsed inward, canvas and metal poles falling like a child's game knocked over. Fadi felt Hassan's body go limp against his shoulder. There was blood on the supply boxes, on Fadi's hands, on the floor where Hassan had been standing. The silence that followed—not the absence of sound, but a particular, suffocating quiet—was worse than the noise. In that silence, Fadi was certain another blast would come. He waited for it with every muscle tensed, breathing shallow, certain that his next breath would be his last.

He was extracted two days later. Hassan was not.

The first months after returning home felt manageable. Fadi threw himself into legislative work with an intensity his colleagues found admirable. He stayed late at the State House, drafted bills on healthcare access, took constituent calls that stretched past midnight. At night, he checked his apartment doors and windows—twice, then three times before bed. It seemed reasonable, given what he had survived. But the checking did not stop. It became ritual: before sleep, after sleep, when returning home from anywhere, sometimes in the middle of the night when he had jolted awake with his heart racing. He told himself he was being prudent, careful. What he did not tell himself was that the checking never relieved the feeling that something was about to happen, that the silence in his apartment meant danger was gathering somewhere just beyond his perception.

Strangers became difficult. At fundraisers and town halls, Fadi found himself gripped by a peculiar dread when introduced to someone he did not know. The handshake, the small talk—these felt precarious, as though the stranger might suddenly say something that would unmake him. When a colleague mentioned military strategy during a committee meeting, Fadi felt the room tilt. He excused himself and did not return. Over months, he began to engineer his life around these moments. He delegated constituent meetings. He avoided certain colleagues. He declined social invitations. The work—the endless, consuming work—was safer. There he could control the narrative, control the outcome.

Now, at sixty-four, Fadi has begun to notice the cost. His reelection campaign is in jeopardy; his absence from community events has been noted. More troubling to him is what happens when he tries to remember that day with any clarity. The memory does not come as a story but as fragments: Hassan's face, the smell, the silence, his own hands covered in blood. When he tries to hold these pieces together, to make them cohere into something he can understand, he is flooded with the same terror that seized him in the tent. His body responds as though the blast is happening now. He has learned to push the memory away, to distract himself, to bury it under work and checking and the small rituals that keep him feeling safe.

What has finally brought him to a therapist's office is quieter than crisis. It is the recognition that the silence he fears most is the one he has created around himself—the isolation that his survival strategies have built, brick by brick. He is afraid that if he stops checking, something will happen. He is more afraid that if he continues, there will be nothing left of his life to protect.
